stops.name: Messina, departure and the storm
stops.campa: On the tenth of April the great fleet — some two hundred ships by the chroniclers' count — puts out from Messina for Cyprus and the Holy Land. A violent storm strikes within days and scatters it across the sea: several vessels are lost outright, and three, including the great ship carrying Richard's bride-to-be, Berengaria of Navarre, and his sister Joan, are driven onto the coast of Cyprus, out of the King's sight and, for some anxious days, out of his knowledge whether they still live.

stops.name: Limassol, the wrecked ships and the tyrant's insult
stops.campa: Isaac Komnenos, the Greek adventurer who has made himself self-styled emperor of Cyprus, plunders the wrecked crews washed onto his shore and refuses the ship carrying Berengaria and Joan leave to take on water, hoping to ransom or seize the women himself. Richard arrives on the sixth of May, hears it, and does not wait for council: he lands his knights through the surf under fire, scatters Isaac's troops on the beach, and takes Limassol before nightfall. Within days the whole conquest of the island — undertaken almost as an afterthought, to punish an insult to two women — is under way.

stops.name: Limassol, the marriage to Berengaria of Navarre
stops.campa: In the small chapel of Saint George within Limassol castle, Richard marries Berengaria of Navarre, whom Eleanor herself had brought south from Spain to meet him at Messina the winter before. The Bishop of Évreux says the mass; Berengaria is crowned Queen of England in the same rite, the only English queen ever crowned outside England. It is a marriage of alliance, made between two campaigns, on conquered ground, with the smoke of the island's subjugation still rising a few miles off — and it will remain, to the end of Richard's life, more a treaty kept than a love matched.

stops.name: Cape Apostolos Andreas, the submission and the silver chains
stops.campa: Isaac's field army breaks near Tremithousa; he runs to the mountain castle of Kantara, and from there down the long horn of the Karpass to the island's last headland, Cape Apostolos Andreas, where the sea ends the road. He surrenders on one condition: that he, an emperor by his own naming, not be bound in iron like a common man. Richard, with the courtesy he can afford a beaten enemy, grants it — and has silver chains made specially to fetter him. Cyprus, taken almost by accident in three weeks, becomes the crusaders' forward base and a Latin kingdom outlasting every mainland conquest of the crusade by three hundred years.

stops.name: Acre, the renewed siege
stops.campa: Richard reaches Acre on the eighth of June, two years into a siege that has itself become a small trapped city — Christian besiegers ringed by Saladin's relieving army, both camps starving under the same sky. Philip Augustus arrived weeks earlier and has made little headway; Richard's engineers and his siege engines, among them a catapult he names Bad Neighbour, change the mathematics of the wall within days. He falls ill soon after landing, with a wasting fever the army calls arnaldia, and directs the siege from a stretcher, having himself carried to the front to loose crossbow bolts at the defenders from his sickbed.

stops.name: Acre, the city falls
stops.campa: On the twelfth of July, after weeks of mining and battery, the garrison of Acre — cut off, its walls broken, no relief able to reach it through the crusader lines — surrenders on terms: the city, its Christian captives, the True Cross taken at Hattin, two hundred thousand gold dinars, and the release of some sixteen hundred named prisoners, all within a month. The banners of England, France, and, over Conrad of Montferrat's objection, of Leopold of Austria, are raised on the walls together. Two years of siege end in an afternoon; the two kings enter the city they have spent their armies to take.

stops.name: Acre, the Duke's banner cast down
stops.campa: Duke Leopold V of Austria, kinsman of the Emperor and the senior surviving prince of the German contingent since Barbarossa's death on the road, sets his own banner beside the royal standards on the walls, claiming a share of a conquest his small force scarcely earned. Richard's men — by some accounts on Richard's own order — tear it down and throw it in the ditch with the filth of the siege camp. It is a small insult, quickly given and quickly forgotten by the man who gave it. Leopold does not forget it, and eighteen months from now the debt will fall due outside Vienna.

stops.name: Ayyadieh, the massacre of the hostages
stops.campa: The deadline for Saladin's ransom passes unmet — the gold short, the Cross not produced, the prisoners not yet freed on his side — and Richard, reading it as bad faith rather than the genuine difficulty it may also be, orders some twenty-seven hundred Muslim captives of Acre led onto the plain of Ayyadieh in full sight of Saladin's watching army and put to the sword. His own chroniclers call it just retaliation for Christian dead; the Arabic sources call it what it plainly also is. Saladin, in answer, kills the Christian prisoners still in his hands. Neither side offers terms again for a long while.

stops.name: Arsuf, the battle in the pines
stops.campa: Marching south along the coast toward Jaffa, shadowed the whole way by Saladin's harrying cavalry, Richard holds his column in tight order through the forest of Arsuf until the Hospitallers at the rear, stung past bearing, break formation and charge without orders. Richard, rather than let the charge be wasted, commits the whole army behind it in a single controlled shock Saladin's line cannot absorb. It is the first open field battle Saladin has lost to a Christian king. Richard, the chroniclers say, is seen everywhere in the melee, unhorsed once, fighting to remount surrounded — Cœur de Lion earning, in one afternoon, the name that outlives him.

stops.name: Jaffa, the port refortified
stops.campa: The army reaches the ruins of Jaffa, razed years before, and Richard sets it building again as the crusaders' forward base and supply port, the hinge between the coast and any march inland toward Jerusalem. He works alongside the masons himself, the chroniclers note, in defiance of royal custom. From here he opens correspondence with al-Adil, Saladin's brother, trading gifts and, eventually, a half-serious proposal that his widowed sister Joan marry al-Adil and the two of them hold a joint kingdom over Jerusalem — a peace by marriage-bed that founders, in the end, on Joan's own fury at being offered as its price.

stops.name: Beit Nuba, the first turning back
stops.campa: By the first days of January the army has fought and marched its way to Beit Nuba, a bare dozen miles from Jerusalem's walls, close enough that scouts ride out and report the very look of the city gates. Then the winter breaks in earnest — cold rain, hail, roads turned to mud that stalls the supply carts — and the council of barons, weighing a siege they cannot supply against a relieving army they cannot yet see, votes to fall back to the coast rather than risk being trapped before walls they might not carry. Richard, who wanted the city as much as any man in the host, gives the order to retreat.

stops.name: Acre, the knighting of the boy al-Kamil
stops.campa: In a lull of the war's diplomacy, al-Adil brings his young son to Richard's camp at Acre — a boy of eleven or twelve, already called al-Kamil, "the Perfect," within his own house. Richard, who has made a courteous friend of the father across a dozen truces and embassies, receives the son with open pleasure, dresses him, and dubs him knight with his own hand in the fashion of the Franks: the accolade, the belt, the spurs. It is a small ceremony between enemies who like each other better than their wars allow them to say, and the boy carries the memory of it into the sultanate he will one day rule.
